The thing about wanting to die, she'd learned, was that it didn't feel dramatic. There was no swelling music, no poetic rain against the window. Just a gray exhaustion that made her bones feel like they were filled with wet sand.

"You did a brave thing calling," the woman said. Her name was Ruth, and she had a slight rasp, like she'd been talking all night.

"It doesn't feel brave," Maya whispered. "It feels like failing at the one thing I'd decided to do."

"Tell me about the last time you laughed."

"See," Ruth said gently. "That version of you still exists. She's just buried under a lot of pain right now. Pain lies, Maya. It tells you it's permanent. It isn't."

"The morning came anyway," Maya said, surprised. "I didn't think I wanted to see it."

"Mornings are stubborn like that," Ruth said. "So are you. You've survived every worst day of your life so far. That's a hundred percent record."
